title: cpu-side-bottlenecks-tokenization-request-parsing-threadpools
content:
Summary:

This note captures a set of CPU-side performance investigations we ran on the serving runtime focusing on the most common hotspots we observed in customer traffic: tokenization, request parsing (JSON/body), thread-pool scheduling overhead, and general Python interpreter overhead (GIL/GC/serialization). The goal is to have an actionable set of mitigations and an experiment plan to reduce median/95th CPU time and request P99 latency for small (<512 token) requests.

Context and why this matters:
- For many production workloads, per-request CPU (host-side) dominates cost/latency for short prompts.
- Even when the model inference is GPU-bound, pre- and post-processing on CPU sets a floor for end-to-end latency and scales poorly during high QPS bursts.
- We've seen customer reports where increasing Dedicated capacity did not reduce P95 because CPU-side work saturated host threads.

What we profiled / environment:
- Release build: serving-runtime v1.8.3 (python worker + C++ middleware)
- Test hardware: c6i.4xlarge-like VM (16 vCPU) used for synthetic load + a Dedicated node (8 vCPU) from prod-like cluster
- Tools: py-spy (flamegraphs), linux perf, eBPF/bcc for syscall tracing, orjson for JSON benchmarks, timeit microbenchmarks, `perf top` on C++ side

Observed hotspots (representative numbers from mixed small-prompt workload):
- Tokenization: 35-50% of CPU time on short requests (1-256 tokens).
    - Python-based tokenizer (pure python loops + regex) = 8-14ms per request for 128-token prompt.
    - HF tokenizers (rust-backed / tokenizers) = 0.7-1.5ms for same prompt.
    - Overhead comes from Python dispatch, string copying, and per-token checks.
- Request parsing + validation (JSON body -> Pydantic models): 10-20% CPU, ~2-6ms per request
    - pydantic.parse_obj and nested model validation are expensive with many optional fields.
    - orjson deserialization is ~2-3x faster than standard json.loads in our microbenchmarks.
- Thread-pool scheduling / task handoff: 8-15% CPU and a source of latency jitter
    - Using an unbounded concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor with many short tasks leads to contention and queue pressure under bursts.
    - Observed worker wake/sleep and context-switch overheads when CPU-bound tokenization tasks run on the Python threadpool.
- Python interpreter overhead / GIL contention: 6-12%
    - When multiple Python threads do tokenization (non C-accelerated), GIL contention causes serialized execution. py-spy shows threads stuck in interpreter time.
- Serialization / response formatting: 3-6% (json.dumps).
- GC pauses minimal but noticeable under allocation-heavy paths (large batch preprocessing).

Microbenchmark snippets (representative):
- Single-threaded 128-token prompt:
    - pure-python tokenizer: median 10.6ms, p95 21ms
    - HF tokenizers (rust c-bindings): median 0.9ms, p95 3.1ms
- JSON parse+validate path (payload with metadata ~1KB):
    - json.loads + manual validation: 4.8ms
    - orjson.loads + manual lightweight validation: 1.6ms
    - pydantic.BaseModel.parse_obj (nested model): 6.3ms

Root causes / analysis:
1) Tokenization implemented in Python for a subset of code paths. For small requests, tokenization dominates CPU.
2) Many code paths do per-request parsing into heavy Pydantic models, but not all fields are used downstream.
3) Threadpool usage: CPU-bound tasks scheduled onto Python threads without using C-level parallelism (Rust/C tokenizers), causing wasted context switches and GIL contention.
4) Some request-serving code paths allocate many short-lived Python objects, causing extra GC/alloc overhead.

Immediate mitigation recommendations (low effort, high ROI):
- Replace json.loads usage with orjson in the hot path. Estimated latency reduction: 1.5-3.2ms per request on parse-heavy endpoints.
- Short-circuit validation: introduce a "fast_path" lightweight decode for common, small requests that avoids full pydantic parsing for fields we don't need. Fall back to full validation when required.
- Adopt HuggingFace tokenizers (rust-backed) or our own C++/Rust tokenizer extension for all serving paths. This reduces tokenization CPU by ~6-12ms per small request.
- Pre-tokenize in the client (when feasible) and accept token arrays (binary) for high-QPS internal customers to avoid tokenization entirely.
- Use uvloop + faster async HTTP stack and ensure we run multiple worker processes (one per 2-4 cores) for CPU isolation.

Medium effort / architectural fixes:
- Move tokenization to C++/Rust extension or a shared microservice that is horizontally scalable and optimized for batching tokenization requests.
- Implement a bounded work-queue and backpressure at the request ingress to avoid unbounded threadpool growth. Configure the threadpool with a fixed worker count and a queue limit.
- Replace pydantic v1 heavy validation with one of: pydantic-core (lighter weight), dataclasses + orjson, or memoized parsed schemas for hot routes.
- Add shared-memory pre-tokenization cache for repeated prompts (prefix caching).

Longer-term experiments (data to collect + metrics):
- Experiment A: Swap tokenizer implementation to HF tokenizers in a canary. Measure: CPU% per request, median latency, P95, throughput at fixed CPU budgets.
- Experiment B: Replace json/pydantic path with orjson + minimal validation for top 5 hot routes. Measure per-route latency and CPU.
- Experiment C: Introduce a tokenization microservice (Rust) behind a local UNIX socket; compare IPC overhead vs Python tokenizer.

Instrumentation and benchmarks to add to CI/CD:
- Add synthetic microbench harness that runs small prompt workload (50ms GPU stall pattern) and measures CPU breakdown with a lightweight profiler.
- Export flamegraph snapshots for key builds and attach to release notes.
- Per-route CPU allocation metrics in Console (tokenization_ms, parse_ms, serialize_ms) and track regression alerts.

Operational knobs to expose (configurable per-deployment):
- tokenizer_impl: [python, hf-rust, external-service]
- parse_mode: [full, fast] (toggle for pydantic vs lightweight)
- threadpool_max_workers and threadpool_queue_limit
- pretokenize_cache_size and pretokenize_ttl

Open questions / unknowns:
- What percentage of real customer traffic can feasibly be pre-tokenized? (requires customer survey / telemetry)
- How much IPC overhead would the tokenization microservice introduce for small requests vs pure in-process rust binding?
- Is pydantic-core migration straightforward given our existing nested models? Need a compatibility pass.

Action items (owners + timeline):
- (Asha) Implement orjson switch in serving hot-path and run canary (1 week).
- (Ben) Spike HF tokenizers integration in a small canary branch + microbench (2 weeks).
- (Lena) Add per-route CPU timing instrumentation to Console and enable for canary routes (2 weeks).
- (SRE) Add bounded threadpool config + default sane limits to runtime config (1 week).

Appendix: quick how-to for reproducing profiling locally
1) Start a local serving instance with DEBUG_PROFILE=1 which enables py-spy sampling and writes /tmp/flame.svg
2) Run the synthetic harness: tools/perf/hotpath_runner.py --profile small-prompts --qps 100 --duration 60s
3) Collect flamegraph: py-spy record -o /tmp/pyflame.svg --pid <pid> --native --format svg
4) For Linux perf on C++: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | flamegraph.pl > /tmp/cpp-flame.svg

Notes from quick experiments
- Switching to orjson dropped parse median by ~2.7ms on our test harness and reduced server CPU by ~7% under mixed load.
- HF tokenizers integration reduced tokenization CPU from ~42% to ~6% in a short spike test (single-node).

Conclusions:
- For short prompts, host-side CPU is dominated by tokenization and request parsing. Replacing Python tokenization and heavy pydantic validation with C-backed tokenizers and lightweight parsing yields the highest immediate wins.
- Operational controls (bounded threadpools, per-route fast-paths) prevent CPU-side saturation during bursts and are low-effort to deploy.

Please review and comment. I'll update this doc with canary results and attach the flamegraphs under linked_artifacts once available.
